Virtual critical points and explicit coefficients

A smooth complex phase may have no real critical point at nearby parameter values. Its stationary expansion is nevertheless determined by a smooth complex graph and finitely many derivatives of the original real-domain functions. We identify every coefficient, including the Jacobian and Gaussian branch, and prove that changing the permitted representatives changes the expansion only by an arbitrarily small power of the frequency.

  • Finite stationary jets and quadratic exchange, Theorems 1 and 3, proves the quadratic expansion and the explicit finite-derivative stationary formula F15. Its general finite-regularity remainder F16 is ; the coefficient comparison below uses a deeper expansion to accommodate that exponent.
  • A matrix estimate with a semipositive imaginary part supplies the full earlier AN-04 matrix argument. Gaussian reduction near a complex critical graph, Sections 2–7, supplies the two contour arguments and their Gaussian expansion. Contour calculus and the Gaussian branch, A1–A4, supplies their determinant identities, square factorization, integration and residue algebra.
  • The real inverse theorem, §§16.4–16.5, and Zero hypersurfaces as curvature measures, Lemma 3.0, prove the inverse and nonlinear change-of-variables results used here. The integration foundation, §§15–16, supplies Fubini and dominated convergence. The scalar foundation, §§12–13, supplies compactness, cutoffs, Taylor estimates and uniform derivative convergence.

Proof. Write the exact division . Extend each coefficient almost analytically. Subtract from . For the inverse statement, write for the actual real inverse, with , and differentiate . Its first derivative at zero is . In a higher derivative, the highest derivative of again has this invertible coefficient. Terms containing only holomorphic derivatives give the formal inverse recurrence. Every other term contains an antiholomorphic jet of , which is flat. Induction gives the asserted comparison. The coefficient functions and their inverses have bounded derivatives on a smaller compact patch; differentiating the induction in parameters retains the flat estimates. The same product-rule argument applies to compositions with amplitudes and to the determinant of the inverse derivative.

Products preserve this flat equivalence. Inverses of nonvanishing scalars or invertible matrices do as well, by subtracting their inverse identities. Nearby scalar roots on the same branch differ by the difference of their squares divided by the sum of the roots. That sum stays nonzero on a sufficiently small patch. These facts justify every rational and root operation below.
